questions.title: Write your own `map`
questions.prompt: Write `map(array, callback)` without using `Array.prototype.map`. Call `callback(item, index, array)` for every item and return a new array of the results. Do not change the original array.
questions.explanation: Create an empty result array, loop over the input with a normal `for` loop, and push `callback(item, index, array)` for each item. Returning a new array instead of changing the input is the whole point: `map` never mutates, which is why React lists use it. Pass all three arguments to the callback; interviewers often check that you pass the index. It runs in O(n).

test_cases.name: passes the array
test_cases.call: map([1, 2], (x, i, arr) => arr.length)

test_cases.name: does not use the built-in map
test_cases.call: (() => { const built = Array.prototype.map; Array.prototype.map = () => { throw new Error("used the built-in map"); }; try { return map([1], (n) => n + 1); } finally { Array.prototype.map = built; } })()

questions.title: Write your own `reduce`
questions.prompt: Write `reduce(array, callback, initial)` without using `Array.prototype.reduce`. Call `callback(accumulator, item, index, array)` for each item. If no `initial` is given, start with the first item. If the array is empty and there is no `initial`, throw a `TypeError`.
questions.explanation: The tricky part is the starting value. If one is given, start the accumulator with it and loop from index 0. If not, start with the first item and loop from index 1, and throw a `TypeError` for an empty array, like the built-in. The solution uses a rest parameter so it can tell "no starting value" apart from a starting value of `undefined`. Each step sets `acc = callback(acc, item, index, array)`.

test_cases.name: sums with a starting value
test_cases.call: reduce([1, 2, 3], (sum, n) => sum + n, 10)

test_cases.name: sums without a starting value
test_cases.call: reduce([1, 2, 3], (sum, n) => sum + n)

test_cases.name: empty array with a starting value
test_cases.call: reduce([], (sum, n) => sum + n, 0)

test_cases.name: empty array without a starting value throws a TypeError
test_cases.call: (() => { try { reduce([], (a, b) => a + b); return "no error"; } catch (e) { return e instanceof TypeError; } })()

test_cases.name: builds an object
test_cases.call: reduce(["a", "b"], (obj, key, i) => ({ ...obj, [key]: i }), {})

test_cases.name: does not use the built-in reduce
test_cases.call: (() => { const built = Array.prototype.reduce; Array.prototype.reduce = () => { throw new Error("used the built-in reduce"); }; try { return reduce([1, 2], (a, b) => a * b, 3); } finally { Array.prototype.reduce = built; } })()

questions.title: `groupBy(items, key)`
questions.prompt: Write `groupBy(items, key)`. It takes an array of objects and a property name, and returns an object where each key is a value of that property and each value is an array of the matching items, in their original order.
questions.explanation: Start with an empty object. For each item, read `item[key]`; if that group does not exist yet, create an empty array for it, then push the item. Because you loop in order and push, each group keeps the original order. Object keys are always strings, so a value of `1` becomes the key "1". It runs in O(n).

test_cases.name: groups by a property
test_cases.call: groupBy([{ type: "fruit", name: "apple" }, { type: "veg", name: "carrot" }, { type: "fruit", name: "pear" }], "type")

test_cases.name: empty array
test_cases.call: groupBy([], "type")

test_cases.name: keeps the original order inside a group
does not change the items
test_cases.call: (() => { const items = [{ g: "x" }]; groupBy(items, "g"); return items; })()

questions.title: `flatten(array)`
questions.prompt: Write `flatten(array)` without using `Array.prototype.flat`. Return a new array with all nested arrays flattened, at any depth. Tip: get one level working first, then make it work for any depth.
questions.explanation: Loop over the items: if an item is an array, flatten it by calling `flatten` on it and push its items with spread; otherwise push the item. That recursion is what handles any depth, because each nested array is flattened before it is added. Empty nested arrays add nothing. A common follow-up is to write it without recursion, using a stack.

test_cases.name: empty array
test_cases.call: flatten([])

test_cases.name: does not change the original
test_cases.call: (() => { const a = [1, [2]]; flatten(a); return a; })()

test_cases.name: does not use the built-in flat
test_cases.call: (() => { const built = Array.prototype.flat; Array.prototype.flat = () => { throw new Error("used the built-in flat"); }; try { return flatten([[1], [2]]); } finally { Array.prototype.flat = built; } })()

questions.title: `memoize(fn)`
questions.prompt: Write `memoize(fn)` for functions that take one argument. It returns a new function that caches the result for each argument, so `fn` runs only once per different argument.
questions.explanation: Keep a `Map` in a closure. On each call, if the cache does not have the argument yet, run `fn` and store the result; then return the cached value. Check with `cache.has(arg)` instead of looking at the value, so falsy results like `0` are cached too. A `Map` keeps `1` and "1" apart, while a plain object would turn both into the key "1".

test_cases.name: caches the same argument
test_cases.call: (() => { let calls = 0; const square = memoize((n) => { calls++; return n * n; }); return [square(3), square(3), calls]; })()

test_cases.name: different arguments run again
test_cases.call: (() => { let calls = 0; const square = memoize((n) => { calls++; return n * n; }); return [square(2), square(3), calls]; })()

test_cases.name: no arguments
test_cases.call: memoize(() => 5)()

test_cases.name: caches falsy results too
test_cases.call: (() => { let calls = 0; const f = memoize(() => { calls++; return 0; }); f(1); f(1); return calls; })()

test_cases.name: 1 and "1" are different arguments
test_cases.call: (() => { const f = memoize((x) => typeof x); return [f(1), f("1")]; })()

questions.title: `debounce(fn, delay)`
questions.prompt: Write `debounce(fn, delay)`. It returns a new function that waits until it has not been called for `delay` ms, then calls `fn` once with the latest arguments and the same `this`. Every new call restarts the wait.
questions.explanation: Keep the timer id in a closure. Every call clears the old timer and starts a new one for `delay` ms, so `fn` only runs once the calls stop. Create the timer inside the returned function so it uses the latest arguments, and call `fn.apply(this, args)` from a regular `function` so `this` is kept. The classic use is a search box that waits for the user to stop typing.

test_cases.name: runs once after a burst of calls
test_cases.call: (async () => { const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); let n = 0; const d = debounce(() => n++, 20); d(); d(); d(); await wait(60); return n; })()

test_cases.name: waits for the delay before running
test_cases.call: (async () => { const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); let n = 0; const d = debounce(() => n++, 50); d(); await wait(10); const before = n; await wait(80); return [before, n]; })()

test_cases.name: uses the latest arguments
test_cases.call: (async () => { const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); let got; const d = debounce((x) => { got = x; }, 20); d(1); d(2); d(3); await wait(60); return got; })()

test_cases.name: each call restarts the wait
test_cases.call: (async () => { const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); let n = 0; const d = debounce(() => n++, 50); d(); await wait(30); d(); await wait(30); const middle = n; await wait(50); return [middle, n]; })()

test_cases.name: separate bursts run separately
test_cases.call: (async () => { const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); let n = 0; const d = debounce(() => n++, 20); d(); await wait(40); d(); await wait(40); return n; })()

test_cases.name: keeps this
test_cases.call: (async () => { const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); let got; const user = { name: "Ann", hi: debounce(function () { got = this.name; }, 10) }; user.hi(); await wait(40); return got; })()

questions.title: `throttle(fn, delay)`
questions.prompt: Write `throttle(fn, delay)`. It returns a new function that calls `fn` right away on the first call, then ignores calls until `delay` ms have passed since the last time `fn` ran. Pass on the arguments and `this`.
questions.explanation: Remember when `fn` last ran. On each call, compare `Date.now()` with that time: if at least `delay` ms have passed, save the new time and run `fn`; otherwise ignore the call. Starting `last` at `-Infinity` makes the first call always run. This is the leading-edge version; a common follow-up is adding a trailing call that runs once the calls stop.

test_cases.name: runs right away on the first call
test_cases.call: (() => { let n = 0; const t = throttle(() => n++, 50); t(); return n; })()

test_cases.name: ignores calls inside the delay
test_cases.call: (() => { let n = 0; const t = throttle(() => n++, 50); t(); t(); t(); return n; })()

test_cases.name: runs again after the delay
test_cases.call: (async () => { const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); let n = 0; const t = throttle(() => n++, 50); t(); await wait(70); t(); return n; })()

test_cases.name: passes the arguments
test_cases.call: (() => { let got; const t = throttle((a, b) => { got = a + b; }, 50); t(1, 2); return got; })()

test_cases.name: runs at a steady rate during constant calls
test_cases.call: (async () => { const wait = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); let n = 0; const t = throttle(() => n++, 50); for (let i = 0; i < 12; i++) { t(); await wait(10); } return n >= 2 && n <= 4; })()

test_cases.name: keeps this
test_cases.call: (() => { const user = { name: "Ann", hi: throttle(function () { return this.name; }, 50) }; return user.hi(); })()

questions.title: `curry(fn)`
questions.prompt: Write `curry(fn)`. The curried function collects arguments over one or more calls. Once it has at least `fn.length` arguments, it calls `fn` with them; until then, it returns a function that waits for more.
questions.explanation: Return a named function, `curried`, that collects arguments. If it has at least `fn.length` of them, call `fn`; if not, return a new function that calls `curried` again with the old and new arguments together. The closure keeps the arguments collected so far, which is why a partial like `add(1)` can be reused. Note that `fn.length` does not count rest parameters or parameters with default values.

test_cases.name: returns a function until it has enough
test_cases.call: typeof curry((a, b) => a + b)(1)

test_cases.name: a partial can be reused
test_cases.call: (() => { const add = curry((a, b) => a + b); const addOne = add(1); return [addOne(2), addOne(10)]; })()

questions.title: Write your own `bind`
questions.prompt: Add `myBind` to `Function.prototype` without using the built-in `bind`. `fn.myBind(thisArg, ...args)` returns a new function that calls `fn` with `this` set to `thisArg`, and with the preset arguments followed by any new ones.
questions.explanation: Inside `myBind`, `this` is the function being bound, so save it as `fn`. Return a new function that calls `fn.apply(thisArg, [...preset, ...args])`: the saved `this`, then the preset arguments, then the new ones. It must not call `fn` right away. A common follow-up is making the bound function work with `new`, where the new object should win over `thisArg`.

test_cases.name: sets this
test_cases.call: (() => { function hi() { return this.name; } return hi.myBind({ name: "Ann" })(); })()

test_cases.name: presets arguments
test_cases.call: (() => { function add(a, b) { return a + b; } return add.myBind(null, 2)(3); })()

test_cases.name: joins preset and new arguments
test_cases.call: (() => { function join(...parts) { return parts.join("-"); } return join.myBind(null, "a", "b")("c", "d"); })()

test_cases.name: does not call the function right away
test_cases.call: (() => { let called = false; function f() { called = true; } f.myBind(null); return called; })()

test_cases.name: returns a new function
test_cases.call: (() => { function f() {} const bound = f.myBind(null); return typeof bound === "function" && bound !== f; })()

test_cases.name: this stays fixed when called as a method
test_cases.call: (() => { function hi() { return this.name; } const bound = hi.myBind({ name: "Ann" }); const other = { name: "Bob", bound }; return other.bound(); })()

test_cases.name: does not use the built-in bind
test_cases.call: (async () => { const built = Function.prototype.bind; Function.prototype.bind = () => { throw new Error("used the built-in bind"); }; try { return await (function () { return this.n; }).myBind({ n: 7 })(); } finally { Function.prototype.bind = built; } })()

questions.title: `deepClone(value)`
questions.prompt: Write `deepClone(value)` for plain objects and arrays. Return a copy where every nested object and array is new, so changing the copy never changes the original. Primitives are returned as they are.
questions.explanation: Return primitives and `null` as they are. Copy arrays with `value.map(deepClone)`, and objects by copying each key with `deepClone` of its value. Recursion makes every nested level a new object, which is the difference from a shallow copy with spread. Check for `null` first, because `typeof null` is "object".

test_cases.name: copies nested objects
test_cases.call: deepClone({ a: { b: 1 }, c: [1, 2] })

test_cases.name: nested objects are new
test_cases.call: (() => { const o = { a: { b: 1 } }; const c = deepClone(o); c.a.b = 2; return o.a.b; })()

test_cases.name: arrays of objects
test_cases.call: (() => { const o = [{ x: 1 }]; const c = deepClone(o); c[0].x = 9; return [o[0].x, Array.isArray(c)]; })()

test_cases.name: primitives and null
test_cases.call: [deepClone(5), deepClone("a"), deepClone(null), deepClone(true)]

test_cases.name: empty object and array
test_cases.call: [deepClone({}), deepClone([])]

test_cases.name: the top level is a new object
test_cases.call: (() => { const o = { a: 1 }; return deepClone(o) !== o; })()

questions.title: Write your own `Promise.all`
questions.prompt: Write `promiseAll(promises)` without using `Promise.all`. Return a promise that resolves with an array of all results, in the same order as the input, or rejects as soon as any one rejects. Plain values count as already resolved.
questions.explanation: Return a new promise, and keep a results array plus a count of how many are left. Wrap each input in `Promise.resolve` so plain values work. When one fulfils, store its value at its own index, not with `push`, so the order matches the input; when the count reaches 0, resolve. Pass `reject` as the error handler, so the first rejection rejects at once. Handle the empty array first, or it would never resolve.

test_cases.name: keeps the input order
test_cases.call: (() => { const later = (ms, v) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms)); return promiseAll([later(30, "a"), later(10, "b"), later(20, "c")]); })()

test_cases.name: empty array
test_cases.call: promiseAll([])

test_cases.name: plain values
test_cases.call: promiseAll([1, Promise.resolve(2), 3])

test_cases.name: rejects with the first error
test_cases.call: promiseAll([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.reject(new Error("boom"))]).then(() => "resolved", (e) => e.message)

test_cases.name: rejects without waiting for the rest
test_cases.call: (async () => { const later = (ms, v) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms)); const start = Date.now(); let message = "resolved"; try { await promiseAll([later(300, 1), Promise.reject(new Error("x"))]); } catch (e) { message = e.message; } return [message, Date.now() - start < 150]; })()

test_cases.name: does not use the built-in Promise.all
test_cases.call: (async () => { const built = Promise.all; Promise.all = () => { throw new Error("used the built-in Promise.all"); }; try { return await promiseAll([1, 2]); } finally { Promise.all = built; } })()

questions.title: An event emitter
questions.prompt: Write a class `EventEmitter` with `on(event, listener)`, `off(event, listener)`, `emit(event, ...args)` and `once(event, listener)`. `emit` calls the event's listeners in the order they were added, with the arguments. A `once` listener runs only one time, and can also be removed with `off` before it runs.
questions.explanation: Store an array of listeners for each event name. `on` pushes, `emit` calls each listener with the arguments, and `off` filters the listener out. In `emit`, loop over a copy of the array, so a listener that removes itself does not make you skip the next one. `once` wraps the listener in a function that removes itself and then calls it; saving the original listener on the wrapper lets `off` remove a `once` listener too.

test_cases.name: emit passes the arguments
test_cases.call: (() => { const e = new EventEmitter(); let got; e.on("add", (a, b) => { got = a + b; }); e.emit("add", 2, 3); return got; })()

test_cases.name: listeners run in order
test_cases.call: (() => { const e = new EventEmitter(); const log = []; e.on("x", () => log.push(1)); e.on("x", () => log.push(2)); e.emit("x"); return log; })()

test_cases.name: off removes a listener
test_cases.call: (() => { const e = new EventEmitter(); let n = 0; const f = () => n++; e.on("x", f); e.emit("x"); e.off("x", f); e.emit("x"); return n; })()

test_cases.name: once runs one time
test_cases.call: (() => { const e = new EventEmitter(); let n = 0; e.once("x", () => n++); e.emit("x"); e.emit("x"); return n; })()

test_cases.name: events are separate
test_cases.call: (() => { const e = new EventEmitter(); let a = 0; let b = 0; e.on("a", () => a++); e.on("b", () => b++); e.emit("a"); return [a, b]; })()

test_cases.name: emit with no listeners does not throw
test_cases.call: (() => { const e = new EventEmitter(); e.emit("nothing"); return "ok"; })()

test_cases.name: removing a listener during emit does not skip the next one
test_cases.call: (() => { const e = new EventEmitter(); const log = []; const first = () => { log.push(1); e.off("x", first); }; e.on("x", first); e.on("x", () => log.push(2)); e.emit("x"); e.emit("x"); return log; })()

test_cases.name: a once listener can be removed with off
test_cases.call: (() => { const e = new EventEmitter(); let n = 0; const f = () => n++; e.once("x", f); e.off("x", f); e.emit("x"); return n; })()
